--- title: "The standard error, derived in three lines" description: "Casella and Berger reach the standard error through variance algebra, before any sampling distribution exists. Every line of that derivation, set against its English and against the R that reproduces it." date: 2026-08-10 categories: - book-revisions tags: - standard error - bootstrap - sampling distribution engine: knitr --- ## Claim The standard error is a distance: roughly how far the estimate sits from the truth, in the units you measured in. If the standard error of the mean is 1.3 centimetres, your 4.2 is typically off by something on the order of 1.3 centimetres. Most introductions reach that number by asking you to imagine drawing the sample again, and again, forever, and then to take the standard deviation of all those imagined means. It is correct, and it is where a large share of readers stop, because the object being described does not exist and never will. You have one sample. You will never draw another. Casella and Berger do not open that way. Section 5.2 of *Statistical Inference* derives the variance of the sample mean before it says anything about the shape of anything, and the standard error is the square root of that variance **(proof)**. No imagined sample appears in the derivation, and none is needed to get the number. ## What it means in English You took twenty-five measurements and averaged them. That average is not the truth. It is off by *something*, and the standard error is an estimate of how big that something usually is — 1.3 centimetres, if your measurements are in centimetres. Four things it is not: - **Not the standard deviation of your measurements.** That describes how spread out the twenty-five were. Collect more data and it stays where it is; the standard error shrinks. - **Not a probability.** On its own it is a distance, and a distance becomes "95 per cent of the time" only once you know the shape of the scatter. - **Not a fact about your sample.** It is a claim about every sample you did not take, made from the one you did take. - **Not something you need a second sample to compute.** That is the whole point of the table below. ## Code, maths, English One row per step, read downward. Left is the R that checks the step — complete enough to run in order, including the object each line needs — middle is the line as the book writes it, right is what that line says out loud. Where a step produces a number, the print follows a `#` and is compared with the prediction beside it, so the arithmetic and the code are seen agreeing rather than taken on trust. **Parameters held fixed.** The true mean is $\mu=1$, the true standard deviation is $\sigma=1$ (so `rexp` is called with `rate = 1 / mu`, which is 1), the sample is $n=25$, and every imagined experiment uses `reps <- 4000` replications. These are the values set in the chunk below, and every printed number in the table is computed from them. ::: {.transition} | Code | Maths | English | |:----------------------|:----------------|:--------------------| | `n <- 25` # sample size
`mu <- 1` # true mean
`sigma <- 1` # true SD
`reps <- 4000` # imagined experiments
`x <- rexp(n, rate = 1 / mu)` # the one sample | $X_1,\dots,X_n$ independent, $\operatorname{E}(X_i)=\mu$, $\operatorname{Var}(X_i)=\sigma^2$ | Every fixed parameter the simulation uses is named here. Twenty-five measurements, each with the same mean and variance. No shape is claimed for them yet. | | `y <- rexp(2000, rate = 1 / mu)` # stand-in data
`var(2 * y) / var(y)` # 4.000 = $a^2$ | $\operatorname{Var}(aX)=a^2\operatorname{Var}(X)$, with $a=2$ | The print is 4.000, the *square* of the constant 2. That square is why the $\frac{1}{n}$ becomes $\frac{1}{n^2}$ two rows down. | | `a <- rexp(2000, rate = 1 / mu)` # first draw
`b <- rexp(2000, rate = 1 / mu)` # independent second draw
`var(a + b) / (var(a) + var(b))` # 1.013 $\approx 1$ | $\begin{aligned}\operatorname{Var}\big(\textstyle\sum_{i=1}^{n}X_i\big)\\&=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{Var}(X_i)\\&=n\sigma^2\quad\text{— Lemma 5.2.5}\end{aligned}$ | The ratio is 1.013: the variance of the sum is the sum of the variances. The check uses two terms to keep it visible; the lemma extends to $n$ terms, giving the $n\sigma^2$ the next row needs. Independence is the only assumption. | | `sigma^2 / n` # 0.040 = predicted variance | $\begin{aligned}\operatorname{Var}(\bar X)&=\operatorname{Var}\big(\tfrac{1}{n}\,\textstyle\sum_{i=1}^{n}X_i\big)\\&=\frac{1}{n^2}\,n\sigma^2\\&=\frac{\sigma^2}{n}\quad\text{— Theorem 5.2.6(b)}\end{aligned}$ | 0.040 is that chain with $\sigma=1$ and $n=25$: pull $1/n$ out squared, add the $n$ variances, cancel one $n$. Every quantity in the line has appeared in a row above it. | | `sqrt(sigma^2 / n)` # 0.200 = $\sigma/\sqrt{n}$ | $\operatorname{SE}(\bar X)=\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}=0.200$ | The square root of the row above. 0.200 is the target the imagined-sample checks below are measured against, and no sample was drawn a second time to get it. | | `m25 <- replicate(reps, mean(rexp(n, rate = 1 / mu)))` # 4,000 imagined samples
`sd(m25)` # 0.199 vs predicted 0.200 | $\operatorname{se}(\bar X)=\sigma/\sqrt{n}=0.200$ | The imagined experiment, run only as a check: 4,000 fresh samples of twenty-five, keep only their means, then measure how far those means scatter. It lands on 0.199 without being told the target — and it is still not how you compute the error from the sample you hold. | | `m100 <- replicate(reps, mean(rexp(4 * n, rate = 1 / mu)))` # 4n
`m400 <- replicate(reps, mean(rexp(16 * n, rate = 1 / mu)))` # 16n
`c(sd(m25), sd(m100), sd(m400))` # 0.199 0.101 0.050 | $\operatorname{se}(4n)=\tfrac{1}{2}\operatorname{se}(n)$; $\operatorname{se}(16n)=\tfrac{1}{4}\operatorname{se}(n)$ | The print runs 0.199, 0.101, 0.050. Quadruple the sample and the error halves; multiply it by sixteen and the error quarters. Double the sample and the error falls by only a factor of $\sqrt{2}$. | | `s <- sd(x)` # SD of the one held sample
`s / sqrt(n)` # 0.223 = $\widehat{\operatorname{se}}$ | $\widehat{\operatorname{se}}=\frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}$ | $\sigma$ is never actually known, so $s$ — the standard deviation of $x$, the sample named in row one — goes in its place. Same arithmetic as row five, using no imagined samples. | | `boot <- replicate(reps, mean(sample(x, replace = TRUE)))` # resample the held sample
`sd(boot)` # 0.218 vs row above | $\sqrt{\frac{n-1}{n}}\cdot\frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}=\sqrt{\tfrac{24}{25}}\cdot\frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}$ | Efron's route: resample the data you already have, 4,000 times. The print is within simulation error of the row above, so the same number arrives with no algebra — which is why he gets the photograph. | | `mean(abs(m25 - mu) <= 1.96 * sigma / sqrt(n))` # 0.957 | $\Pr\big(\lvert\bar X-\mu\rvert\le 1.96\,\sigma/\sqrt{n}\big)\approx 0.95$ | **Not** the derivation. Coverage needs the shape of the scatter, which §5.3 and §5.5 supply; here it reaches 95.7 per cent. The check has to reach for `m25`, the imagined samples, because one sample cannot show coverage on its own. | ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Where this comes from **The derivation.** Casella & Berger, *Statistical Inference*, 2nd ed., §5.2 "Sums of Random Variables from a Random Sample": Lemma 5.2.5 (the variance of a sum of independent terms) and Theorem 5.2.6(b) ($\operatorname{Var}\bar{X} = \sigma^2/n$, p. 214). The sampling distribution of $\bar{X}$ is §5.3; the central limit theorem is §5.5. The book does not use the words "standard error" until §10.1.4, "Bootstrap Standard Errors", p. 478 — §5.2 stops at the variance, and taking the square root is the step every applied text adds. **The bootstrap.** Efron, B. (1979), "Bootstrap methods: another look at the jackknife", *Annals of Statistics* 7(1), 1–26. For the mean, the nonparametric bootstrap variance is $\frac{n-1}{n}\cdot\frac{s^2}{n}$, which is where the $\sqrt{(n-1)/n}$ comes from. **The photograph.** Bradley Efron receiving the National Medal of Science, 2007. Photograph by Ryan K. Morris, National Science and Technology Medals Foundation, released by the NSF into the public domain; via Wikimedia Commons. Cropped to a portrait, nothing else altered. :::
